questions.prompt: What kind of communication relationship does the delegate pattern create?

options.text: A one-to-one link between a sender and a single receiver.
options.explanation: Delegation connects one sender directly to one delegate object.

options.text: A one-to-many broadcast to all active view controllers.
options.explanation: A one-to-many broadcast describes NotificationCenter, not delegation.

options.text: A global queue that stores messages on disk until read.
options.explanation: Delegation is an immediate in-memory pattern, not a disk queue.

options.text: A many-to-many mesh network between all data models.
options.explanation: Delegation is strictly a one-to-one relationship.

questions.prompt: Why should a delegate property almost always be marked with the weak keyword?

options.text: Because weak references execute their methods on background threads.
options.explanation: Weak references do not affect the thread on which methods run.

options.text: Because a strong reference creates a retain cycle when both objects hold each other.
options.explanation: When an owner holds a child and the child holds a strong delegate to the owner, a retain cycle occurs.

options.text: Because Swift protocols cannot be used with strong property references.
options.explanation: Swift protocols can be strong, but doing so for delegates creates memory leaks.

options.text: Because weak properties automatically convert all return values into optionals.
options.explanation: Weak refers to memory ownership, not method signature return types.

questions.prompt: When is a closure callback preferred over setting up a full delegate protocol?

options.text: When sending messages between two separate running applications on iOS.
options.explanation: Closures cannot cross process boundaries between separate apps.

options.text: When the communication requires five different lifecycle callback methods.
options.explanation: When handling multiple related callbacks, a delegate protocol is cleaner.

options.text: When handling a single asynchronous response or simple user action callback.
options.explanation: Closures are ideal for quick, single-action completion handlers.

options.text: When the caller must receive broadcast events from ten different sources.
options.explanation: Broadcasting to multiple sources is best handled by NotificationCenter.

questions.prompt: Which pattern is best suited for broadcasting user logout to multiple unrelated screens?

options.text: A delegate protocol assigned to every visible view controller.
options.explanation: A delegate can only link to one object at a time, not broadcast to many.

options.text: A chain of nested closures passed down through every subview.
options.explanation: Passing closures down deep view hierarchies creates tight coupling.

options.text: A global variable that all views poll every second using a timer.
options.explanation: Polling global variables with timers wastes battery and adds latency.

options.text: A notification broadcast posted through NotificationCenter to all observers.
options.explanation: NotificationCenter provides decoupled one-to-many broadcast messaging.

questions.prompt: Why must a delegate protocol inherit from AnyObject in Swift?

options.text: To allow the delegate property to be declared with the weak keyword.
options.explanation: Only class-bound protocols conforming to AnyObject can be marked weak.

options.text: To allow struct types to conform to the delegate protocol as values.
options.explanation: Conforming to AnyObject forbids value types like structs from conforming.

options.text: To force all delegate methods to run on the main thread automatically.
options.explanation: AnyObject does not influence thread scheduling.

options.text: To enable Objective-C runtime compatibility across older operating systems.
options.explanation: Use @objc for Objective-C compatibility; AnyObject is pure Swift.

questions.prompt: On which thread does NotificationCenter execute observer callbacks by default?

options.text: Always on the main queue to keep user interfaces responsive.
options.explanation: NotificationCenter does not automatically dispatch to the main queue.

options.text: On the thread that called the post method to broadcast the notification.
options.explanation: NotificationCenter delivers notifications synchronously on the poster thread.

options.text: On a private background thread managed directly by the kernel.
options.explanation: NotificationCenter does not switch threads on its own during post.

options.text: On the thread where the observer originally registered its listener block.
options.explanation: The observer block runs on the caller thread unless specified via an operation queue.

questions.prompt: What happens if you do not remove a block-based notification observer token?

options.text: The compiler issues a warning and prevents the app bundle from building.
options.explanation: The Swift compiler does not enforce token removal at compile time.

options.text: iOS automatically purges the token whenever the device enters low power mode.
options.explanation: iOS does not purge NotificationCenter observer tokens automatically.

options.text: The observer closure remains active in memory and continues receiving events.
options.explanation: Block-based observer tokens persist until explicitly removed or released.

options.text: The posting object throws an exception during its next notification post.
options.explanation: Posting never throws exceptions for unremoved observer tokens.

questions.prompt: How can an escaping closure that references self avoid creating a retain cycle?

options.text: By wrapping the closure body inside an autoreleasepool block.
options.explanation: Autoreleasepool manages Objective-C autoreleased objects, not Swift ARC cycles.

options.text: By marking the enclosing class instance with the final keyword modifier.
options.explanation: The final keyword prevents subclassing, but does not alter ARC capture.

options.text: By calling DispatchQueue.main.async inside every closure statement.
options.explanation: Dispatching asynchronously does not break strong capture cycles.

options.text: By adding [weak self] or [unowned self] to the closure capture list.
options.explanation: Capture lists tell ARC to capture self weakly, preventing retain cycles.

questions.prompt: Can a notification observer return a value directly back to the notification sender?

options.text: No, notifications are a one-way fire-and-forget broadcast mechanism.
options.explanation: NotificationCenter posts events one-way and cannot return values to the caller.

options.text: Yes, by specifying a non-void return type in the notification name.
options.explanation: Notification names are string identifiers and do not have return types.

options.text: Yes, by writing a synchronous completion handler in the userInfo dictionary.
options.explanation: Posting does not wait for or return values from observer closures.

options.text: No, unless both sender and observer run on the same actor isolation.
options.explanation: Notifications are one-way regardless of concurrency or actor isolation.

questions.prompt: Which communication pattern allows two-way questions, such as asking if a row may be deleted?

options.text: NotificationCenter broadcast posts.
options.explanation: NotificationCenter is one-way and cannot return decision answers.

options.text: The delegate pattern using protocol methods.
options.explanation: Delegates can return values (such as Bool) back to the sender.

options.text: UserDefaults key-value change notifications.
options.explanation: UserDefaults KVO is an observation tool, not a two-way question protocol.

options.text: Global error handling with try and catch.
options.explanation: Throwing errors handles failures, not conversational decision questions.

questions.prompt: What is a major architectural downside of relying heavily on NotificationCenter?

options.text: It prevents unit tests from compiling in Xcode projects.
options.explanation: Unit tests can easily post and observe notifications.

options.text: It uses up to ten times more device battery than closures.
options.explanation: NotificationCenter has negligible battery impact compared to closures.

options.text: It hides control flow and makes dependencies hard to trace.
options.explanation: Broadcasting obscures which components listen and react to specific events.

options.text: It forces all data models to be written as Objective-C classes.
options.explanation: NotificationCenter works natively with Swift structs and classes.

questions.prompt: What modern Swift concurrency feature provides an alternative to block-based NotificationCenter tokens?

options.text: Iterating over notifications using an AsyncSequence with for await.
options.explanation: NotificationCenter.default.notifications(named:) returns an AsyncSequence.

options.text: Marking notification names with the Sendable protocol modifier.
options.explanation: Sendable ensures thread safety, but does not replace the observation mechanism.

extension Notification.Name {
    static let ping = Notification.Name("ping")

questions.prompt: Compare delegates and closures in iOS. Explain when you would choose each pattern and how memory management differs.

rubric.criterion: Explains that delegates represent formal one-to-one contracts for multiple events or two-way queries, while closures suit single asynchronous callbacks or simple events.
Explains memory management: delegates require weak properties and AnyObject protocols, while closures require capture lists such as [weak self] to prevent retain cycles.
Contrasts architectural trade-offs: delegates offer explicit protocol contracts and mockability; closures provide inline brevity and reduced boilerplate.

questions.modelAnswer:
Delegates and closures both provide one-to-one communication, but they serve different architectural needs.

I choose a delegate when communication involves multiple related lifecycle events. It also fits two-way questions, such as asking if a table row can be deleted. A delegate defines a formal protocol, making contracts explicit and easy to mock in unit tests. Memory management requires marking the delegate property as weak and constraining the protocol to AnyObject.

I choose a closure for a single event or asynchronous completion callback, like a network download. Closures keep call sites concise without extra protocol definitions. For memory management, escaping closures stored on self must use a capture list with [weak self] to prevent retain cycles.

questions.prompt: What is NotificationCenter, when is it appropriate to use, and what are its key architectural risks?

rubric.criterion: Defines NotificationCenter as a one-to-many broadcast mechanism suitable for decoupled events like user sign-out or keyboard frame changes.
Identifies risks: synchronous delivery on the caller thread causing background UI crashes, and memory leaks from forgotten observer tokens.
Discusses architectural downsides: hidden dependencies, untyped userInfo dictionaries, and difficult control flow tracing.

questions.modelAnswer:
NotificationCenter is a one-to-many broadcast mechanism managed by Foundation. A sender posts a notification without knowing who receives it, and zero or more observers react independently.

It is appropriate for global, app-wide events where components should not be tightly coupled. Examples include user logout, keyboard appearance, and system memory warnings.

Its key architectural risks include:
1. Threading: Post runs synchronously on the caller thread. If posted from a background queue, observers run in the background, risking UI crashes if not dispatched to main.
2. Memory leaks: Block-based observer tokens must be explicitly retained and removed, or they leak and continue listening.
3. Coupling and maintenance: Notifications obscure control flow and use untyped userInfo dictionaries, making data dependencies hard to debug.

questions.prompt: Explain how retain cycles happen with both delegates and closures, and explain how to prevent them in Swift.

rubric.criterion: Explains how delegate retain cycles form when parent and child hold strong references to each other, and shows how weak var breaks it.
Explains how closure retain cycles form when an object stores an escaping closure that captures self strongly, and shows how [weak self] breaks it.
Mentions that delegate protocols must be class-bound with AnyObject to permit weak storage.

questions.modelAnswer:
A retain cycle happens when two objects hold strong references to each other, preventing ARC from releasing their memory.

With delegates, a retain cycle occurs when a parent view controller owns a child component. If the child holds a strong delegate reference back to the parent, both stay in memory. To prevent this, constrain the delegate protocol to AnyObject and declare the delegate property as weak var.

With closures, a retain cycle occurs when an object stores an escaping closure in a property, and that closure references self. The object owns the closure, and the closure strongly captures self. To prevent this, add a capture list with [weak self] to the closure definition, turning the captured reference into an optional.

questions.prompt: Why does NotificationCenter post notifications synchronously, and what threading bug often results from this behavior?

rubric.criterion: Explains that NotificationCenter delivers notifications synchronously on the current thread where post was invoked.
Explains that background notification posts cause observers to run in the background. UI updates will crash unless dispatched to the main queue.

questions.modelAnswer:
NotificationCenter delivers notifications synchronously on the thread where post is called. When post executes, NotificationCenter iterates through all registered observers on that exact thread and runs their selectors or closures before returning control to the poster.

A frequent threading bug occurs when background operations, like network tasks or database queries, post a notification. Observers that receive the notification execute on that background thread. If an observer updates views directly without dispatching to the main queue, issues arise. The app risks race conditions and main thread crashes.

questions.prompt: How does Swift modern concurrency change how iOS developers observe notifications and handle asynchronous callbacks?

rubric.criterion: Mentions NotificationCenter.default.notifications(named:) returning an AsyncSequence that can be iterated with for await without manual token cleanup.
Explains how async/await replaces nested escaping completion closures with structured linear code and compile-time concurrency checking.

questions.modelAnswer:
Modern Swift concurrency simplifies both notification observation and asynchronous callbacks.

For notifications, Swift introduces NotificationCenter.default.notifications(named:), which returns an AsyncSequence. Instead of registering block tokens and manually removing them in deinit, developers iterate over notifications using a standard for await loop inside a structured Task. When the Task cancels, observation stops automatically without memory leaks.

For asynchronous callbacks, async/await replaces escaping completion handler closures. Methods return values or throw errors directly instead of passing Result types through closures. This eliminates deep callback nesting, avoids accidental forgotten completion calls, and provides compile-time data race safety through Swift actors.
